title: A Story of Numbers: Number Systems Through History
seo_title: A Story of Numbers Class 8 Worksheet with Answers (Ganita Prakash Part 1, Chapter 3)
standard_code: Class 8, Ganita Prakash Part 1, Chapter 3: A Story of Numbers
standard_text: The development of number systems: counting and grouping, Roman and Egyptian numerals, place-value systems in other bases (2, 5 and 60) and the Indian place-value system with zero (summary of NCERT Ganita Prakash Class 8)
meta_desc: Class 8 A Story of Numbers worksheet (Ganita Prakash Part 1, Chapter 3): Roman numerals, Egyptian numbers, base 2, base 5, base 60 and the Indian place-value system. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Place value: each place is worth base × the place to its right
key_sub: With a zero symbol, ten digits are enough for every number.
body_html:
How it works

Early systems added symbols: Egyptian numbers repeat a symbol for 1, 10, 100, 1,000 … Roman numerals also subtract: IV = 4, XC = 90.

A place-value system in base b has places worth 1, b, b², b³ … from the right. Base 2 uses only 0 and 1: 1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11. The Mesopotamians used base 60.

The Indian system is base 10 with a symbol for zero, so any number can be written with ten digits.

Example

What is 10110 in base 2?

Places 16, 8, 4, 2, 1

16 + 4 + 2

Answer: 22

Example

Write 94 in Roman numerals.

90 = XC

4 = IV

Answer: XCIV

Common mistakes

  • Adding every Roman symbol: IX is 9, not 11.
  • Reading 101 in base 2 as one hundred and one. It is 4 + 1 = 5.
  • Thinking zero is just ‘nothing’. In a place-value system it holds a place.

faq.a: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1,000. Symbols are added, but a smaller symbol before a larger one is subtracted (IV = 4).
A place-value system with only the digits 0 and 1; the places are worth 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 …
It lets a place be empty, so the same ten digits can write every number in a place-value system.
